papers.title_in_file: Extreme Events of Quantum Walks on Graphs
papers.version_note: arXiv:2502.19355v1, dated February 27, 2025; 7 pages of main text and references plus 7 pages of Supplementary Material.
papers.what_it_is: A numerical and analytic study of extreme events (exceedences above a degree-dependent threshold) of discrete-time quantum walks on ring lattices and scale-free graphs, compared with classical random walks.

existing.note: The paper says more: with degenerate eigenvalues both the mean and the standard deviation differ from classical values and the flux-fluctuation relation is no longer linear; the case shown is the Grover coin, whose eigenvalues plus and minus one are highly degenerate. The claim rests on a numerical example (Fig. 2(b), SM Fig. 6).
existing.value: The authors state that when the walk operator has degenerate eigenvalues, the second term of the time-averaged evolution also contributes, the DTQW strongly deviates from the classical walk, both the mean and the standard deviation of the flux differ from the classical values, and the flux-fluctuation relation is no longer linear; they show this for the Grover coin, which has large degeneracy at the eigenvalues plus and minus one.
existing.anchor: Main text after Eq. 9, Fig. 2(b), p.3; SM Section V, Fig. 6, p.12
quotes: However in the case of degenerate eigenvalues, the the second term also contributes to the time-averaged ⟨z⟩ at a vertex.
Then, the DTQW strongly deviates from the classical walk.
Both ⟨zv⟩ and σz significantly differ from corresponding classical values, and the fluxfluctuation relation is no more linear.
This can be seen in the case of DTQW with Grover coin (in Fig. 2(b)) which has large degeneracy for the eigenvalues ±1
existing.certainty_reason: Shown by one numerical example (Grover coin on one scale-free graph); no proof for the degenerate case.

existing.value: The authors derive a quantum flux-fluctuation relation (Eq. 8): the standard deviation of the flux at a vertex is approximately its mean flux divided by the square root of 2E, where E is the number of edges; the standard deviation part assumes non-degenerate eigenvalues of U and an initial state that is a uniform superposition over all the edges, and the non-degeneracy makes the cross term vanish.

assertions.value: The authors study discrete-time quantum walks generated by linear unitary evolution on a ring lattice and a scale-free graph whose degree distribution falls as k to the power minus 2.3, and compare them with classical random walks.
assertions.anchor: Abstract, p.1; main text, pp.1 to 2
quotes: We consider quantum walks on a ring lattice and a scale-free graph.
In this work, we focus on large amplitudes of discrete time quantum walks (DTQW) generated by linear unitary evolution.
results for QW on a scale-free (SF) graph with degree distribution P (k) ∼ k−2.3, and on a ring graph
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its scope (abstract and p.2).

assertions.value: The paper defines the discrete-time quantum walk as the unitary U = SC applied to the initial state, with C a coin and S a shift; on a general graph the walk lives on the 2|E|-dimensional space of directed edges, the shift swaps the amplitudes on an edge, and the coin is block diagonal with a unitary of order equal to each vertex's degree.
assertions.anchor: Main text p.1 and Eqs. 2 to 3, p.3; SM Section I, p.8
quotes: unitary operation U = SC applied on the initial state ψ(t = 0) representing the walker, where C and S represent a coin and a shift operation [47]
the quantum walk takes place in a complex vector space C2|E| spanned by the basis eij representing the edge be- tween vertices i and j
so as to swap the amplitudes on the edges
where each Ci is a unitary matrix of order ki, degree of i-th vertex
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own definition of the model (p.1, p.3).

assertions.value: The authors use the Fourier coin (a generalization of the Hadamard coin to arbitrary size) and the Grover coin with the edge-swap shift, to show how results depend on the coin spectra; they state their analytic results depend only on the spectral properties of U and not on the choice of shift operator.
assertions.anchor: Main text p.3; SM Section I.a, p.8
quotes: our analytical results depend solely on the spectral properties of U and hence are not limited by this choice of the shift operator
For the numerical results we use the shift operator in Eq. 2 in combination with Fourier and Grover coins to demonstrate the dependence on the coin spectra.
The Fourier coin is a generalization of the Hadamard coin to arbitrary size
assertions.certainty_reason: The setup is stated; the independence from the shift is an author's claim.

assertions.value: The paper defines an extreme event for the quantum walk as the probability density at vertex i exceeding a threshold equal to its time-averaged mean plus m standard deviations, and the extreme event probability as the probability of that exceedence, by analogy with the classical definition for walkers.
quotes: extreme event is based on the condition zi(t) > ziee, where the threshold is ziee = ⟨zi⟩ + mσz
Corresponding extreme event occurrence probability for DTQW is: Fiq = prob(zi > ziee). (10)
where wiee = ⟨wi⟩ + mσi, with m ∈ R, represents vertex-dependent threshold for extreme events
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own definition (Eq. 10, p.4).

assertions.value: The authors state that the quantum extreme event probability does not appear to be analytically tractable from the distribution of z, so they estimate it from finite time series.
quotes: In principle, Fiq can be obtained from the distribution of z, which does not appear to be analytically tractable.
we estimate Fiq from finite time series of zi(t)
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own stated limit of its method (p.4).

assertions.value: The authors state that in all simulations all walkers start at one node and evolution up to t = 2000 is discarded as transient; the quantum walk starts localized at one vertex in the walker comparison.
quotes: In all simulations reported here, all the W walkers at time t = 0 are initially placed at one node and evolution up to t = 2000 are ignored as transients.
Next, DTQW is executed on the same graph with initial state ψ(0) = δ(0).
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its simulation setup (p.2).
assertions.reader_inference: The 2000-step transient is stated for walkers; the text does not say whether the same cut applies to the quantum time series.

assertions.value: The authors report that on a scale-free graph the probability density of the quantum walk at a vertex looks like a stochastic process although the dynamics is unitary and deterministic, and its distribution is wider than the classical walker distribution; on a ring the quantum fluctuations appear more correlated.
quotes: it has the characteristics of a stochastic process though the underlying dynamics is unitary and deterministic
even this cursory visual examination shows that the width of the distribution is larger for the DTQW compared to that of the CRW
we observe a similar but possibly more correlated fluctuations
assertions.certainty_reason: A visual observation from one simulation (Fig. 1).

assertions.value: The authors state that for classical random walks the flux-fluctuation relation (Eq. 1) is exactly solvable and holds on any graph, in the limit that each degree is much smaller than 2E, with mean flux W times k over 2E.
quotes: For CRW, this is an exactly solvable problem.
in the limit that ki << 2E = N i=1 ki
where ⟨wi⟩ = W ki . 2E (1)
This result in Eq. 1, called the flux-fluctuation relation, is satisfied by CRW on any graph.
assertions.certainty_reason: A known classical result restated without proof in this paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The relation for the standard deviation in Eq. 1 is printed flat in the text layer (a square root is lost), so it is not restated here.

assertions.value: The authors report (Table I) that for the DTQW on periodic lattices of size N = 729 in 1 to 3 dimensions the mean flux is nearly identical to the classical walk, while the standard deviation deviates from the classical result.
quotes: As observed in Table I for a DTQW with periodic boundary condition on regular lattices in 1- to 3-dimensions, ⟨z⟩ is nearly identical to that of CRW, though σz deviates from the classical result.
The sizes of the 1D, 2D and 3D lattice is N = 729.
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulation result in one table.

assertions.value: The paper states and proves, following Aharonov et al., that the time-averaged probability at any vertex converges to the sum over spectral idempotents of the expectation of F_r D_v F_r; the proof uses the spectral decomposition of U and requires non-degenerate eigenvalues so the cross terms vanish.
assertions.anchor: SM Section II, Theorem and proof, p.9; main text Eq. 5, p.3
quotes: Theorem Let F1, F2, . . . , Fm be the spectral idempotents of the transition matrix U . Let |x⟩ be the initial state, then for any vertex v, the time average probability at the node v converges to r⟨x|FrDvFr|x⟩.
if the eigenvalues are non-degenerate, the above term converges to zero as T goes to infinity. Hence the only term that survives is r FrDvFr.
In this, Fr are the spectral idempotent of U , and U is assumed to have a non-degenerate eigenspectrum.
assertions.certainty_reason: A theorem attributed to [47] (Proof [47]); its proof is reproduced, but it is a cited result.
assertions.reader_inference: The theorem's statement on p.9 omits the non-degeneracy condition; it appears only in its proof and in the main text.

assertions.value: The authors derive (Eq. 6) that the time-averaged probability at a vertex, averaged over vertices of the same degree k, is k over 2E plus a correction of order one over E squared, for a uniform or a localized initial state, so the mean density is proportional to degree as for classical walks; the derivation assumes the eigenvector weights average about 1/M.
assertions.anchor: Main text Eq. 6, p.3; SM Section III, pp.9 to 11
quotes: = 2E + O E2 , (6) v∈Sk where Sk = {v ∈ V |deg(v) = k}
This equation states that the mean probability density (at a vertex with de- gree k) is proportional to degree of the vertex being con- sidered.
where we used the assumption that ∥vir∥2 ≈ 1/M on average
Hence, under the assumptions made above, the relation between time-averaged probability at a node of given degree k
assertions.certainty_reason: An approximate derivation under stated heuristic assumptions; the equation is printed flat in the text layer.
assertions.reader_inference: Here M = 2|E|, so k over M equals k over 2E.

assertions.value: The authors report that for the Fourier coin on a scale-free graph with N = 1000 vertices the fitted slope between standard deviation and mean is 1.60 × 10−2, consistent with the expected 1.50 × 10−2.
quotes: Mean flux ⟨z⟩ vs. standard deviation σz for DTQW on a scale-free graph with N = 1000 vertices (circles); (a) DTQW with Fourier coin
has slo√pe 1.60 × 10−2, consistent with the expected slope of 1/ 2E ∼ 1.50 × 10−2
assertions.certainty_reason: One simulation fit on one graph.

assertions.value: The authors report (Table II, lattices of size 729, threshold m = 3, 100 classical walkers) that the classical extreme event probability is 0.1283 in 1D, 2D and 3D, while the quantum one is 0.0202, 0.0135 and 0.0109, decreasing as dimension increases because the quantum standard deviation changes with dimension.
assertions.anchor: Main text Table II and discussion, p.4
quotes: The sizes of the 1D, 2D and 3D lattice is 729. The total number of walkers for the CRW is 100, while the thresholds for EE was set at m = 3.
Hence, Fq for QW decreases as dimensionality of lattice increases.
Thus, even when the graph dimension increases, Fic remains invariant as seen in Table II.
assertions.certainty_reason: Numerical estimate from one set of simulations.
assertions.reader_inference: The text says the quantum standard deviation increases with dimension, but Table I prints 0.149, 0.078 and 0.061 (decreasing); the stated direction and the table disagree.

assertions.value: The authors report that on a scale-free graph with N = 1000 the quantum extreme event probability decays as a power law in degree, with a threshold-dependent exponent of about 0.17 − 0.1m in the text (0.17 − 0.09m in the figure caption), reminiscent of the classical walk.
assertions.anchor: Main text and Fig. 3 caption, p.4
quotes: The EE probabilities decay as a power-law with degree Fiq ∼ kγm , with threshold dependent exponent γm ≈ 0.17 − 0.1m.
This is reminiscent of a similar trend for the CRW case [44].
where the scaling relation was numerically found to be Fiq ∼ kγm , where γm = 0.17 − 0.09m
Now, let us examine the extreme event probability on SF graph with N = 1000.
assertions.certainty_reason: A numerical fit on one graph.
assertions.reader_inference: The text and the caption give different slopes (0.1 against 0.09); the exponent's sign is lost in the text layer.

assertions.value: The authors report that scaled extreme event probabilities for different thresholds collapse onto one curve, which they read as the decay trend being independent of the choice of threshold.
quotes: as displayed in the inset of Fig. 3, we observe a good collapse of all the curves onto one
This implies that the decay trend of extreme event probability is independent of the choice of threshold.
assertions.certainty_reason: Numerical result on one graph.

assertions.value: The authors state that the scale-free graph used for Fig. 3 has exactly one node of degree 71, the highest, and 505 nodes of degree 2, the smallest; for the classical walk only the m = 3 threshold is shown.
quotes: There is exactly one node of degree 71 (highest) while there are 505 nodes of degree 2 (smallest).
For CRW, we show only the m = 3 threshold results for visual clarity
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own description of its test graph (Fig. 3 caption).

assertions.value: The authors report that on a scale-free graph the density time series at neighbouring vertices show no significant cross-correlation and the autocorrelation decays exponentially, so z behaves like a stochastic process, while on a ring lattice the cross-correlations are significant and sustained and the autocorrelation saturates at a non-zero value.
quotes: Figure 4(a,b) does not reveal any significant correlation, and Cij(τ ) → 0 as the shortest path between i and j gets longer.
The auto-correlation C00(τ ) in Fig. 4(c) shows exponential decay of correlation profile implying that z(t) behaves as though it is a stochastic process
reveals significant correlations between two pairs of vertices
Figure 4(f) shows that C00(τ ) saturates at some non-zero value
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulations on graphs of 100 nodes.

assertions.value: The authors report that phases at neighbouring vertices are strongly correlated on both scale-free and ring graphs, while the phase autocorrelation at a vertex decays exponentially on the scale-free graph and faster than exponentially on the ring.
quotes: which reveal strong phase correlations among neighboring vertices
However, the autocorrelation shown in Fig. 5(b,d) decays exponentially (on SF graph) and is faster than exponential decay (on ring graph).
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulation on graphs of 100 nodes.

assertions.value: The authors explain the classical-like extreme event statistics by the local dynamics: the extreme event probability depends only on the time series at one vertex, which on the scale-free graph behaves like a nearly uncorrelated stochastic process; they infer extremes of the phase would give similar results.
quotes: the extreme event probability for QWs, shown in Fig. 3, depends on dynamics of zi(t) on i-th vertex, irrespective of the nature of dynamics on other lattice points
we might infer that the local dynamics of z(t), on SF graph, behaves similar to a nearly-uncorrelated stochastic process with an exponential auto-correlation function
even for extremes in phase variable θ, we could have obtained similar results
assertions.certainty_reason: An interpretation the authors draw from the correlation plots.

assertions.value: The authors report that for the Grover coin, where the flux-fluctuation relation fails, the distribution of extreme event recurrence times is still exponential, which they attribute to null correlation between density time series; the dependence of mean recurrence time on degree is affected.
assertions.anchor: SM Sections V to VI, Figs. 6 to 8, pp.12 to 13
quotes: the distribution of recurrence times is still a nice exponential as shown in Fig. (8)
the null correlation between time-series of squared probability amplitudes is a sufficient condition for obtaining an exponential recurrence-time distribution
dependence of the average recurrence time on the degree of a vertex is affected for the case of DTQW with Grover coin
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulation on one scale-free graph of 1000 nodes.

assertions.value: The authors note that the non-degeneracy assumption comes from Aharonov et al. and that literature links the high eigenvalue degeneracy of the Grover coin to partial localization.
quotes: Aharonov et. al. [47] made an assumption that the spectra of the unitary evolution operator is non-degenerate
It has been noted in literature that such a degeneracy leads to partial localization [50, 51].
assertions.certainty_reason: Attributed to cited work.

assertions.value: The authors sketch a scheme in which the probability density of the vertex time series is tied to the distribution of eigenvalue-pair phase differences of U (Eqs. 14 to 16), assuming a certain factor is almost uniform over eigenvalue pairs and approximating the sum by an integral for a large unitary.
assertions.anchor: SM Section VII, Eqs. 14 to 16, pp.12 to 14
quotes: we can in principle obtain the PDF of time-series at a node in closed form by inverting the above expression
If we assume this factor f to be almost uniform as you vary r and s.
Equations(16) and (14) together capture the dependence of the PDF on the spectral properties of the evolving unitary via the two-point distribution function Ω
assertions.certainty_reason: A sketched approximate scheme, not carried to a closed form.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that extremes can arise even in a phase coherent phenomenon with linear quantum dynamics, and that as far as extreme events are concerned the results are qualitatively similar to classical random walks.
quotes: This work shows that extremes can arise even in phase coherent phenomenon with linear quantum dynamics.
surprisingly, at least as far as extreme events are concerned the results have qualitative similarity to that of classical random walks
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's conclusion from simulations and approximate derivations.

papers.version_note: arXiv:2305.01874v1 [cond-mat.stat-mech], 3 May 2023; 5 pages of main text and references plus a supplement to p.21.
papers.what_it_is: A method (TNMP) that computes marginals of Boltzmann distributions on graphs by contracting tensor networks inside local neighborhoods and passing cavity messages between them, tested on Ising and spin glass models on synthetic, power grid and lattice graphs.

quotes: In the figure, we can see that TNMP gives much smaller errors than belief propagation, the method in [16], and MCMC with a large number of updating steps.
using a spin glass model (with random ±1 couplings and random fields) on the real-world electric power grid network [30] containing n = 494 nodes

existing.note: The body states the exactness condition more precisely than the abstract: the environment approximation is exact when the boundary tensors are not connected through tensors outside the neighborhood (the environment factorizes); limited treewidth governs the cost of contracting the neighborhood, not exactness. The paper argues this; it gives no formal theorem.
existing.value: The authors state that the rank-one (product) approximation of the environment is exact when the boundary tensors of a neighborhood are not connected by tensors outside it, and a good approximation when they are connected only by long loops; when every neighborhood's environment decomposes this way, contracting cavity networks layer by layer gives the marginal exactly. The cost of contracting a neighborhood depends on its treewidth.
existing.anchor: Main text, TNMP, p.2; SM The TNMP equations, p.8; main text p.3
quotes: The approximation is exact if a, b, and c are not connected by tensors outside Ni, and is a good approximation if they are connected only by long loops via tensors outside Ni.
we can contract the cavity networks layer by layer from the boundary of the entire network to Ni, then the result is exactly Pi
The computational complexity of computing the local variable by contracting the neighborhood depends on the treewidth of the neighborhood graph.
existing.certainty_reason: An argued exactness condition, not a stated theorem with proof.

quotes: The problem has the same complexity as computing the partition function and falls into the class of #P problems in mathematics, so there is no polynomial algorithm that solves the problem exactly in general.
It is well known that computing Z is a #P problem so there is no polynomial algorithm to solve it.
existing.certainty_reason: Background statement about the field, not proved in the paper.
existing.reader_inference: Saying #P implies no polynomial algorithm assumes a complexity separation the paper does not state.

assertions.value: The paper's problem is computing local observables such as marginals and magnetizations of a Boltzmann distribution over binary spins on a graph, with pairwise energy terms and external fields at inverse temperature beta.
quotes: Consider statistical mechanics problem defined on a graph G with n vertices and a set of m edges E, and binary configurations s ∈ {+1, −1}n, which follow Boltzmann distribution
where β is the inverse temperature
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own problem statement (p.1).

assertions.value: The authors state that message passing works well only on locally tree-like graphs and can be inaccurate or fail to converge with short loops, while tensor network contraction is exponential in treewidth and only works for small systems without translational invariance because of long loops.
quotes: message-passing algorithms can be inaccurate and even fail to converge due to short loops
working well only on locally tree-like graphs without many short loops
the exact contraction of the whole tensor network has computational complexity exponential in the treewidth of the graph [25]
for systems without translational invariance tensor networks only apply to small systems
assertions.certainty_reason: Statements about prior methods, with citations.

assertions.value: The paper defines TNMP: the marginal of node i is computed by contracting the tensors in a neighborhood of i together with cavity tensors on its boundary, the environment is approximated as a tensor product of the cavity tensors (assuming they are independent), and the cavity tensors are computed iteratively as in message passing.
assertions.anchor: Main text, Tensor Network Message Passing, p.2
quotes: tensor network contractions are responsible for contracting short loops while message passing is responsible for long loops
we introduce a rank-one approximation of the environment as a tensor product of all cavity tensors
which assumes independence between the cavity tensors
We compute the cavity tensors iteratively, analogous to computing cavity messages in message-passing algorithms.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own definition of its method (p.2).

assertions.value: The paper builds each neighborhood by adding neighboring tensors until the minimum distance between every pair of boundary tensors, measured by shortest paths through tensors outside the neighborhood, is at least a given value R; larger R gives a larger neighborhood and a more accurate computation.
assertions.anchor: Main text p.3; SM Constructing the neighborhoods, pp.10 to 11
quotes: subject to that the minimum distance min(ab) dab(∂Ni) between all pairs of tensors (a, b) on the boundary ∂Ni not smaller than a given value R
defined as the length of the shortest path connecting a and b only via the tensors outside Ni
a larger minimum distance results in a more accurate computation of local variables
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own definition of the neighborhood (p.3).
assertions.reader_inference: The claim that larger R is more accurate is argued, not proved; see the lattice trade-off assertion.

assertions.value: The authors show that on a tree TNMP with direct-neighbor neighborhoods reduces to belief propagation, and that if a neighborhood spans the whole network the computation is exact and equals the conventional tensor network method, so the algorithm generalizes both.
quotes: so we can generate Ni simply using the direct neighbors of i, and TNMP reduces to belief propagation in this case
then d(∂Ni) = ∞ and the marginal computation is exact, which is actually the conventional tensor network method
In this sense, our algorithm generalizes both the tensor network method and belief propagation.
assertions.certainty_reason: An argument from the construction, not a numbered theorem.

assertions.value: The authors state that a neighborhood with small treewidth is contracted exactly with a good contraction order, and one with large treewidth with the approximate CATN algorithm; TNMP converges once and gives consistent environments for all local observables.
quotes: If treewidth is small, we use exact tensor network contraction by finding a good contraction order
If the treewidth is large, we employ an approximate contraction algorithm that works for arbitrary tensor networks [20].
TNMP only needs to converge once, giving all consistent environments
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own description of its method (p.3).

assertions.value: The authors test on a ferromagnetic Ising model on a synthetic graph of n = 1000 nodes, a random graph of average degree d = 2 with cliques of sizes 2 to 9 added, at temperature T = 2.0 and external field h = 0.1; exact magnetizations come from contracting the whole network with dynamic slicing and multi-GPU computation.
assertions.anchor: Numerical experiments, p.3; Fig. 2 top caption, p.4
quotes: we randomly generated a network with n = 1000 nodes, random links with d = 2, and cliques with sizes ranging from 2 to 9
The temperature of the model is fixed at T = 2.0 and the external field h = 0.1.
with the help of the dynamic slicing and multi-GPU computation
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own experiment setup (pp.3 to 4).

assertions.value: The authors report that on the synthetic graph the TNMP error decreases monotonically with R, equals belief propagation at R = 0, beats the Cantwell and Newman loopy method at the same maximum neighborhood size, with the gap growing at R = 3, 4 and 5, and reaches an error smaller than 10−7 with a maximum neighborhood size of 666.
assertions.anchor: Numerical experiments, Fig. 2 top, pp.3 to 4
quotes: the error of our method decreases monotonically with R. With R = 0, our method reduces to belief propagation and gives the same result.
our method gives better results. The difference becomes larger with R = 3,4, and 5.
We can see that our method works to the maximum neighborhood size as large as 666, giving an error smaller than 10−7.
assertions.certainty_reason: One experiment on one synthetic graph.

assertions.value: The authors report that the MCMC error decreases slowly with the number of Metropolis-Hastings steps, reaching 10−4 at ten to the seventh steps on the synthetic graph.
quotes: We see that the error decreases slowly with a larger number of steps, obtaining 10−4 with 107 steps.
assertions.certainty_reason: One experiment.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer prints the step count flat; it reads as ten to the seventh.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Cantwell and Newman method (without Monte Carlo sampling) has cost exponential in neighborhood size, so they restrict it to R of 5, while TNMP's cost depends on neighborhood treewidth; they contract exactly for R < 9 and use CATN for R ≥ 9.
quotes: method (without employing Monte-Carlo sampling) is exponential in the neighborhood size (as labeled in the figure), which increases rapidly with R so in the evaluation, we restrict it to 5
we use exact tensor network contraction with R < 9. For R ≥ 9 the neighborhood sub-tensor-networks are very large so we use CATN method [20] to contact them
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own experiment setup (p.4).

assertions.value: The authors report that on the 494-node power grid spin glass all neighborhoods could be contracted exactly, the largest containing 250 nodes, and for R larger than 16 the TNMP error drops to rounding error, so TNMP is exact with a maximum neighborhood smaller than the 494 nodes.
quotes: With all R values, in TNMP we can always contract sub-tensor networks exactly, even when the largest neighborhood contains 250 nodes.
when R is larger than 16, the error of our method drops to the rounding error
TNMP is exact even when the maximum neighborhood size is smaller than the number of nodes 494
assertions.certainty_reason: One experiment on one graph.

assertions.value: The authors state the power grid spin glass uses couplings of plus or minus one with equal probability, Gaussian random fields, and temperature T = 2.0.
quotes: random-interaction and random- field spin glass model on the real-world network of bus power system [30] at a fixed temperature T = 2.0
The coupling J are chosen as ±1 with equal probability
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own experiment setup (Fig. 2 caption).

assertions.value: The authors report that on a ferromagnetic Ising model on the same power grid the results are qualitatively similar to the spin glass, and with R = 5 the TNMP mean magnetization coincides well with the exact result across temperature.
assertions.anchor: SM More results, Fig. S12, pp.19 to 21
quotes: The results are qualitatively similar to that the TNMP behavior on the spin glass model on this graph.
We can see that with R = 5, TNMP performs coincides very well to the exact results.
assertions.certainty_reason: One experiment on one graph.

assertions.value: The authors report that at the same R the TNMP neighborhoods are larger than Cantwell and Newman's, reflecting different meanings of R, and that at large R on the power grid many neighborhoods exceed 200 nodes, which needs an efficient contraction algorithm.
assertions.anchor: SM Constructing the neighborhoods, Figs. S5 and S6, p.11
quotes: we can see that the neighborhood sizes of TNMP are larger than that of Cantwell and Newman with the same R
there are more and more large neighbors with sizes greater than 200, which calls for an efficient algorithm for contracting the neighborhood tensor network
assertions.certainty_reason: Measured on the test graphs.

assertions.value: The authors show that, because the networks contain many copy tensors, each cavity tensor can be represented by a message vector and a copy tensor, reducing space complexity; they state this holds only with many copy or diagonal tensors and not, in general, for expectations in quantum systems.
quotes: the cavity tensor pa→Ni can be equivalently represented as the contraction of a message vector ma→Ni and a copy tensor
We notice that his simplification is valid only in the case of existing many copy or diagonal tensors
For the application of our method in other problems such as computing expectations in quantum systems this simplification does not hold
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own stated limit of the simplification (SM p.10).

assertions.value: The paper gives an algorithm: convert the model to a tensor network, choose each neighborhood, build cavity sub-networks, initialize every message vector to (0.5, 0.5), iterate local contractions until the maximum change falls below a criterion, then contract each neighborhood with the converged environments to get marginals.
quotes: Initialize all the message vectors ma→i(t = 0) for every boundary-center pair to (0.5, 0.5)

papers.what_it_is: A theory and simulation paper proving that similar class-average encoded states force a cross-entropy loss floor near ln K, showing three data conditions under which amplitude encoding produces such concentration, and testing it on synthetic, EuroSAT and MNIST data.

existing.value: The paper proves three concentration results for amplitude encoding: if all feature elements share a sign and their magnitudes are nearly equal, each encoded state is close to the uniform superposition state; if the elements are i.i.d., zero-mean and symmetric, the expected encoded state is the maximally mixed state; and if the two classes' element densities are mirror images, the two classes' expected states are identical.
